title: How to Test Indoor Air Quality at Home
h1: How Do I Test the Air Quality in My Home?
description: Learn how to test indoor air quality at home with monitors and test kits for particles, CO2, VOCs, humidity, radon and mold, and how to read what you find.
quick_answer: Start with a home air quality monitor that tracks particles (PM2.5), carbon dioxide, VOCs, temperature and humidity, and leave it running for a week or more in the rooms you use most. Add carbon monoxide alarms, a radon test kit if you want to check for radon, and a professional inspection for suspected mold or persistent problems.
body:
What should I test for?

Indoor air isn't one thing. Different pollutants come from different sources, and each one needs its own kind of test. The main ones to think about in a Southern California home are:

  • Fine particles (PM2.5) from cooking, dust, candles and wildfire smoke
  • Carbon dioxide (CO2), which rises when rooms aren't getting enough fresh air
  • VOCs, chemicals that come from paint, cleaners, furniture and building materials
  • Humidity, which affects mold, dust mites and comfort
  • Carbon monoxide from gas appliances, furnaces and attached garages
  • Radon, a natural radioactive gas from soil
  • Mold, usually tied to a moisture problem

Are home air quality monitors accurate enough?

For spotting trends, yes. Consumer monitors aren't lab instruments, but a decent one will show you when particle levels spike, when CO2 builds up in a closed room, and whether humidity is too high or low. That's usually enough to find the source and see whether your fixes are working.

A few tips for getting useful readings:

  1. Pick a monitor with a laser particle sensor and a true CO2 sensor (often labeled NDIR). Cheaper "eCO2" readings are estimates.
  2. Place it at breathing height, away from windows, vents, the kitchen stove and direct sun.
  3. Leave it running for at least a week so you see normal patterns, not one moment.
  4. Move it between rooms, starting with bedrooms and the main living area.
  5. Note what you were doing when readings spike, like cooking, vacuuming or running the dryer.

How do I test for carbon monoxide, radon and mold?

Carbon monoxide: don't rely on a general air monitor. Install dedicated CO alarms near sleeping areas and on every level of the home, and test them monthly. California requires CO alarms in homes with gas appliances, fireplaces or attached garages. If one sounds, get everyone outside and call 911.

Radon: short-term test kits are sold at hardware stores. You place the kit in the lowest lived-in level for a few days and mail it to a lab. Radon levels vary by location, so a simple test is the only way to know for your home.

Mold: DIY mold test plates aren't very helpful, since mold spores are present almost everywhere. If you see mold, smell mustiness, or have had a leak, focus on finding the moisture. A professional inspection makes sense when you can't find the source.

What do the readings mean?

Most monitors color-code their results, but here's a rough guide to what's normal:

ReadingWhat to aim forCommon cause when high
PM2.5Low and steady, with short spikes only during cookingCooking, smoke, dust, poor filtration
CO2Close to outdoor levels when rooms are aired outClosed rooms, not enough fresh air
VOCsLow baselineNew furniture, paint, cleaners, stored chemicals
HumidityRoughly 30 to 50 percentCoastal marine layer, showers, leaks

Look for patterns more than single numbers. A reading that stays high all day points to a constant source, while short spikes usually line up with an activity.

What should I do if the results are bad?

Match the fix to the problem:

  • High particles: upgrade the HVAC filter, use a range hood that vents outside, and consider a whole-home air cleaner. During Santa Ana winds and wildfire smoke, keep windows closed and run the system fan with a good filter.
  • High CO2: open windows when outdoor air is clean, leave bedroom doors cracked, or talk to a pro about adding fresh air ventilation.
  • High VOCs: remove or air out the source, store chemicals in the garage, and choose low-VOC products.
  • High humidity: use bath and kitchen fans, fix leaks, and consider a dehumidifier in damp coastal homes.

If readings stay poor after the easy fixes, the HVAC system may be part of the problem. Dirty or leaky ducts and a dirty coil can spread pollutants through the house. Our indoor air quality team can inspect your system and suggest filtration, UV lights, ventilation or humidity control that fits. If you need a visit, you can request a free estimate.
faqs: What is the best way to test indoor air quality?

For most homeowners, a quality monitor that tracks PM2.5, CO2, VOCs and humidity is the best starting point. Pair it with CO alarms and a radon test kit, and bring in a professional if you suspect mold or problems persist.
How long should I run an air quality monitor?
At least a week, and longer if you can. That captures daily routines like cooking, sleeping and cleaning, so you can tell a constant problem from a short spike.
Can wildfire smoke affect indoor air?

Yes. Fine smoke particles get indoors through gaps, open windows and leaky ducts. Keep windows closed, use the best filter your system can handle and run a portable HEPA purifier in bedrooms during smoke events.
Do I need a professional air quality test?
Not always. A home monitor answers most questions. A professional visit helps when you suspect hidden mold, have unexplained symptoms, or want your HVAC system checked as a source.
When Should You Have Your Indoor Air Quality Tested?

Consider testing indoor air quality when you notice musty odors, visible mold or symptoms that improve when you leave the house, after water damage, a remodel or wildfire smoke, and when you buy or move into a home. Every home also needs working carbon monoxide alarms, since CO can't be seen or smelled.
What Is an Indoor Air Quality Assessment, and What Does It Check?

An indoor air quality assessment is an evaluation of the air in your home and the things that affect it. A technician asks about symptoms and concerns, measures conditions like humidity, particles and carbon dioxide, inspects the HVAC system, filters and ducts, looks for moisture and odor sources, then explains the findings and options.
